title: Chronicle of Important Events

rows: The Emperor Jimmu ascended the Throne at the Kashiwara Palace, Unébiyama, Yamato province, near the present Nara.
Neighbouring clans subdued by the armies of the Imperial Princes.
The Great Shrine of Isé built by the Emperor Suinin in honour of Amatérasu-Omikami.
Clans and tribes in Kyushu and the eastern half of the Main Island subdued by the armies of the Emperor Kéiko and Prince Yamatotakéru his son.
The Emperor Séimu divided his dominion into administrative districts.
The Emperor Nintoku established the capital at Naniwa (Osaka) for the convenience of intercourse with Korea.
Japanese Office in Mimana is destroyed by Silla.
Imperial Prince Shotoku became Regent, and propagated Buddhism, building Horyuji and other temples.
The Regent Shotoku proclaimed the Constitution.
The Asuka or Empress Suiko's Period of Art history.
The custom of 'year-names' introduced, the first one being called Taika (great reformation).
Ézo (Hokkaido) subjugated by the army of Hirafu Abé.
Control over the Korean Peninsula abandoned.
The Taiho Law promulgated and the organization of the Imperial Government is fixed.
The Hakuho Period of Art history.
6. Establishment of the Capital at Nara and Compilation of a History of Japan.
The Empress Gemmyo founded Nara as her capital.
The first books of Japanese history, Nihon Shoki (Japanese Annals) and Kojiki (Antiquities) compiled.
7. Spread of Buddhism and Progress of Religious Fine Art.
Building of Todaiji temple and other provincial temples.
The Empress Kōmyo donated the treasures of the late Emperor Shomu to Todaiji temple. They are kept in the Shosoin Museum, built a little later.
Dictatorship of Dōkyo, Buddhist pope, opposed by the great loyalist Kiyomaro Waké.
The Tempyo Period of Art history.
8. Founding of Héian (Kyoto) the Capital, and troubles in the north.
The Emperor Kammu founded the new capital Héian and the Government removed there from Nara.
Revolts broke out in Ézo, finally subdued by the expedition of Tamuramaro Sakanoué.
Establishment of governmental and private schools.
The Konin period of Art history.
Mototsuné Fujiwara the Daijo Daijin and Regent became Kampaku (Chief Councillor) at the same time.
Michizané Sugawara, candidate for Kampaku reduced to the position of governor of Kyushu by the Fujiwara scandal.
Official intercourse with Tang broken off by the advice of Michizané Sugawara.
Bokkai, a maritime monarchy in Manchuria, traded with Japan.
11. Disorder in Rural Districts and Rise of the Samurai.
Masakado Taira rebelled and proclaimed himself Emperor.
Sumitomo Fujiwara disturbed the coasts of the Inland Sea but is suppressed.
The Samurai families of Minamoto (Genji) and Taira (Héishi or Héiké) gradually rose to power.
Michinaga Fujiwara assumed the Regency for the next 20 years and his son Yorimichi for 50 years. Climax of the Fujiwara despotism and prosperity.
Toi tribe in the north-eastern part of Korea invaded the islands of Iki and Tsushima.
Tadatsuné Taira's treason in Shimoosa province.
Armies of Buddhist monks rose in revolt.
The Abés in the Ohu district declared independence.
The ex-Emperor Shirakawa took part in politics for nearly 40 years and set a precedent for government by ex-Emperors.
The Ohu district again disturbed by the Kiyowaras.
For about a century the family of Kiyohira Fujiwara who subdued the Kiyowaras ruled over the Ohu district.
Strife between the armies of the Emperor and the ex-Emperor (Hogen war).
The Fujiwaras and Minamotos waged war against another branch of the Fujiwaras and the Tairas (Héiji war).
Kiyomori Taira promoted to Daijo Daijin.
Autocracy of Kiyomori and his family.
Rise of the Minamotos in rivalry to the Tairas. Yoritomo Minamoto established headquarters at Kamakura.
The Tairas destroyed by the armies of Yoshitsuné, brother of Yoritomo.
Yoritomo appointed local military police and tax-gatherers for rural districts.
The Fujiwara Period of Art history.
15. Beginning of the Kamakura Shogunate Régime.
Yoritomo Minamoto promoted to Séii-Taishogun (Generalissimo) and the Shogun Government formally sanctioned. For the next 675 years Japan ruled by the samurai statesmen.
Tokimasa Hojo became chief executive of the Shogunate régime.
Minamoto Shogunate ended with the third Shogun, Sanétomo. But Masako, widow of Yoritomo, (called the 'Ama' or Nun Shogun) officiated as Shogun for several years.
Trouble between the Kyoto Court and the Hojos (Shōkyu affair).
Yasutoki Hojo became chief executive of the Kamakura Shogunate.
The Hojos continued to exercise the Shogun's duties for over a century.
The Joéi Code promulgated for the discipline of the samurai.
Second Yuan invasion and defeat by the armies of Tokimuné Hojo, the chief executive.
An attempt for the restoration of the Imperial Rule.
War between the Imperial and the Hojo armies.
17. The Emperor Godaigo and Takauji Ashikaga.
Temporary restoration of the Imperial direct rule by the Emperor Godaigo.
Takauji Ashikaga rebelled against the Emperor.
Masashigé Kusunoki, famous loyalist, died in the battle of Minatogawa (Kobé).
The Emperor Godaigo moved to Yoshino mountain.
The Imperial House divided into two, the South and the North (Yoshino and Kyoto) for 57 years.
The Kamakura period of Art history.
18. Beginning of the Muromachi Shogunate and the luxurious age of Yoshimitsu.
Takauji Ashikaga proclaimed himself Shogun and established the Muromachi Shogunate in Kyoto.
Takauji sent the Tenryuji-buné (trade boats) to China.
Yoshimitsu Ashikaga publicly appointed Shogun and the Muromachi Shogunate officially sanctioned.
Yoshimitsu traded with Ming: indulged in luxurious living.
19. Corruption of the Muromachi Shogunate and Political Commotion.
The Éikyo Rebellion. Rising of military lords in Kanto district.
The Ohnin war: Kyoto reduced to ashes in the street fighting. The Court and the Shogunate both lost power and the whole country became a scene of warfare among the military lords.
20. A Century of Civil Wars Among the Feudal Lords.
Soun Hojo captured Odawara Castle and ruled over the Kanto district.

Feudal lords struggled for supremacy, the greater lords being as follows: Kanto district; Hojo, Uésugi. Ohu district; Daté, Ashina, Mogami, Tamba, Akita. Central district; Uésugi, Takéda, Imagawa. Kinki (Kyoto-Osaka) district; Saito, Asai, Asakura, Oda, Matsudaira. Chugoku (Western Main Island) district; Ukida, Amako, Ohuchi, Mori. Shikoku Island; Miyoshi, Kono, Chosokabé. Kyushu Island; Otomo, Ryuzoji, Shimazu.
The Muromachi Period of Art history.
Nobunaga Oda came up to Kyoto by Imperial order and repaired the Palace.
Nobunaga destroyed Énryakuji temple to suppress the power of the monks.
Hidéyoshi promoted to be Kampaku and Daijo Daijin.
Unity of the Empire realized by Hidéyoshi, all the lords completely subdued.
Invasion of Korea by armies of Toyotomi.
Hidéyoshi Toyotomi died at Fushimi castle (Momoyama Palace).
The Momoyama period of Art history.
Battle of Sékigahara assured the supremacy of Iyéyasu Tokugawa (1542-1616).
Iyéyasu appointed Shogun and founded the Yédo Shogunate.
The Loochoo Islands subjugated by Lord Shimazu.
Sending of official letters to Nova-Hispania and Spain.
Iyéyasu prohibited the preaching of the Catholic Faith.
The lord Masamuné Daté sent Hasékura to Rome.
The Toyotomis destroyed at the Battle of Osaka.
Proclamation of the Kugé Hatto (Court Nobles Law) and the Buké Hatto (Samurai Law).
Iyémitsu (1604-1651) became the third Tokugawa Shogun. Under his enlightened rule the position of the Yédo Shogunate became unshakable.
Death of Iyémitsu and attempted rebellion by Yuino Shosétsu and his colleagues.
24. The Golden Age of the Yédo Shogunate.
Mitsukuni Tokugawa, lord of Mito began the compilation of the Dai Nippon Shi (Great Nippon History).
The Shogun Tsunayoshi's Edicts for the protection of animals caused much loss of human life.
The Genroku Era of luxurious living.
The 8th Shogun Yoshimuné regulated officialdom and improved the administration, reigned for 30 years.
Yoshimuné loosened the Prohibition Law against Western books.
Punishment of Takénouchi Shikibu, a loyalist.
Norinaga Motoori commenced his commentary on the Kojiki (Antiquities).
Misrule of the Roju Okitsugu Tanuma.
Adjustment of the administration by the Roju Sadanobu Matsudaira (Rakuo).
Punishment of Shihéi Rin (Hayashi) who warned the Government of possible invasion by foreign Powers.
Coming of an English boat to Nagasaki.
Shogunate order to shut out all foreign ships by force.
Great famine of the Tempo Era.
Rebellion of Héihachiro Oshio to relieve the starving masses.
Coming of the American ship Morrison.
The Roju Tadakuni Mizuno's attempt at reformation.
The 1825 order removed. A step towards the 'open door' policy.
Controversies between the anti-foreign party and the liberalists became hotter.
King of Holland gave advice to the Shogunate.
First request of America for the 'open door.'
Arrival of the American fleet under Commodore Perry.
Coming of the Russian delegate Poutiatine to Nagasaki.
Institution of the Sun Flag to symbolize Japan. (Sanctioned by the Meiji Government in 1870.)
Conclusion of Amity Treaties with America, England and Russia.
Conclusion of Amity Treaty with Holland.
Arrival of the American envoy Townsend Harris.
Conclusion of Commercial Treaties with Foreign nations by the Shogunate.
The Anséi coup d'État by the Tairo Naosuké Ii.
The Japanese envoy Masaoki Niimi sent to America.
The Tairo Ii assassinated at the Sakurada gate of the Shogun Palace.
The Anti-Foreign Law, and attack on foreign ships at Shimonoséki and Kagoshima.
Defeat of the Anti-Foreign party; the seven Court nobles flee to Nagato.
The Anti-Foreign party demanded the release of the seven Court nobles by force; battle at the Hamaguri gate of the Kyoto Imperial Palace.
A combined fleet of America, England, France and the Netherlands bombarded Shimonoséki.
Imperial Sanction given to the treaties of 1858.
Hostilities between the Shogunate forces and the army of the Choshu (Nagato) Lord who represented the Anti-Shogunate and Anti-Foreign Party.
Ascension of the Meiji Tenno (1852-1912), the 122nd Emperor.
The Emperor ordered armies opposed to the Nagato Lord to withdraw.
Rapid progress of Anti-Shogunate movement and a definite scheme promoted by Sanjo, Iwakura, Saigo, Okubo and Kido.
The Emperor gave orders to the lords of Nagato and Satsuma to move their armies against the Yédo Shogunate in compliance with the request of Sanjo, Iwakura and their colleagues, October 14.

On the same day (October 14) the Shogun Yoshinobu Tokugawa asked Imperial sanction for the return of all authority of the Government to the Throne. On October 24 the Emperor complied with his request and accepted Yoshinobu's resignation.

The rise of the lords and warriors loyal to the Shogunate. Battle of Toba-Fushimi. March of the Imperial armies to Yédo. Surrender of the Yédo Castle without bloodshed. Battles at Uéno, Utsunomiya and Aizu.
Battle at Hakodaté, May, after which all disturbances in the wake of the political change completely subdued.
The Yédo period of Art history.
The first year of Meiji, beginning with September.
Proclamation of the Five Imperial Pledges.
Removal of the Capital to Tokyo.
Surrender of fiefs by the lords.
Japan is divided into 1 "Dō," 3 urban prefectures and 72 prefectures for administrative purposes. (The number being reduced in 1889 to the present 1 Dō, 3 urban prefectures and 43 prefectures.)
The people allowed to cut off their cues and the samurai forbidden to wear swords.
Institution of the national school system.
The Loochoo Islands definitely included within Japanese territory.
Opening of railway line between Tokyo and Yokohama.
Institution of the Conscription system of military service.
Request for opening the House of Representatives.
First Convention of the local governors.
Kumamoto incident, a reactionary movement by the Jimpuren band of Kumamoto Samurai. Similar events occured at Akitsuki and Hagi.
The South-Western Civil War, the rebellion of Takamori Saigo and his colleagues.
Rapid influx of things and ideas from Europe, called Rokuméi-kan period.
Imperial Edict promising the opening of the national assembly.
Hirobumi Ito sent to Europe for the study of Western constitutional governments.
Japan became a member of the International Red Cross Society.
Institution of city, town and village divisions.
Proclamation of the Dai Nippon Téikoku Kempo (The Constitution of the Great Empire of Japan), Feb. 11.
The First Imperial Diet convened in November.
Issuance of the Imperial Rescript on Education.
Institution of the system of courts of justice and promulgation of court procedures.
The Three Powers' Intervention and return of the Liaotung Peninsula to China.
Battle of the Japan Sea, May 27.
Promulgation of the Revised Penal Code.
Revision of Treaties with Western countries on equal footing.
Demise of the Emperor Meiji, July 30.
Ascension of the Emperor Taisho, July 30.
New Treaty with China. So-called '21 Demands'.
End of the World War, November.
The South Sea Islands mandated to Japan.
Japan became a member of the League of Nations.
Great Earthquake of Kanto district, September 1.
Conclusion of Treaty with the U. S. S. R.
Promulgation of the new Election Law (Universal Suffrage).
Demise of the Emperor Taisho, December 25.
Ascension of the present Emperor, December 25.
Outbreak of the Manchurian Incident, September 18.
Withdrawal from the League of Nations, March.
The World Economic Conference at London.
Manchoukuo became an Empire with Kangte (Mr. Pu Yi) as first Emperor, March 1.
Japanese Government notified the U.S. Government their intention to terminate the Washington Naval Treaty, December 29.
Japan withdrew from the London Naval Conference, January 15.
The 'February 26 Affair' (assassination of three political dignitaries, M. Saito, K. Takahashi, and General J. Watanabé).
Beginning of the China Incident, July 7.
Beginning of the fight in Shanghai, August 13.
Complete occupation of Shanghai by the Japanese Army, November 10.

title: Chronological Index of Principal Events
caption_extra: For the convenience of reference a chronological index of principal events in the country's foreign relations is appended :

rows: Arrival of first American civil envoy, Townsend Harris.
Harris concluded convention with the Shogunate.
A Russian fleet seized the island of Tsushima but abandoned it shortly afterwards through the intervention of Great Britain.
A British fleet bombarded Kagoshima city.
A combined fleet of Great Britain, the United States, France and the Netherlands bombarded Shimonoséki.
Treaties with Britain, France, the Netherlands, Russia and the United States were sanctioned by the Emperor.
Prince Iwakura's mission left for the United States and Europe.
Similar Treaties concluded with other Powers.
Japanese Government seized Peruvian slaver "Maria Luz" in Yokohama.
Japan sent a punitive expedition to the island.
EXCHANGE OF SAGHALIEN AND THE KURILE ISLANDS
Japan ceded Saghalien to Russia in exchange for the Kurile Islands.
The United States recognized Japan's territorial sovereignty over the Bonin Islands.
Count Ito and Li Hung-chang signed the convention defining Sino-Japanese relations in Korea.
Japan guaranteed the non-alienation of Fukien province from China.
Treaty signed in Washington, D. C. on Feb. 11.
Sino-Japanese convention embodying relevant terms of Portsmouth Treaty signed.
EXCLUSION OF JAPANESE SCHOOL CHILDREN IN CALIFORNIA
Movement started in California for exclusion of Japanese children from common schools.
New Agreement concluded allowing Japan complete supervision of Korean domestic administration.
Japan exchanged on Dec. 3 a memorandum with Canada in connection with the immigration problem.
Official Notes exchanged regarding the preservation of peace in the Far East.
An agreement signed on Aug. 15 between Japan and China regarding the Antung-Mukden Railway.
PROPOSAL TO NEUTRALIZE THE SOUTH MANCHURIA RAILWAY
Japan refused on Jan. 21 to accept the proposal of Secretary of State Knox of the United States regarding neutralization of the South Manchuria Railway.
A new agreement concluded on July 4 between Japan and Russia regarding the maintenance of the status quo in Manchuria.
Japan notified Great Britain and 10 European countries on July 17 that existing treaties would be revised a year later. On August 4, similar notices served to France and Austria-Hungary.
Japan signed the International Copyright Treaty in Berlin on September 8.
FRANCO-JAPANESE AGREEMENT REGARDING PATENTS AND COPYRIGHT
An agreement concluded on May 8, regarding patents and copyright in China.
Treaty concluded on the basis of the arbitration treaties between Great Britain and the United States.

The United States published revised treaty with Japan on April 5. Great Britain, Spain, and Sweden did likewise on April 6, May 15 and July 13 respectively. Italy, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Canada published revised treaties with Japan simultaneously on July 15, followed by Germany, Austria-Hungary and France on July 16, August 3, and August 26 respectively.
ANTI-JAPANESE ALIEN LAND LAW IN CALIFORNIA
Passage of the so-called Webb Bill.
Negotiations regarding the Kunchow, Hankow and Nanking incidents concluded on October 7, the Chinese accepting all the Japanese demands.
A treaty concluded between Japan and China regarding the railway building concessions.
Japan recognized the Republic of China on October 6 simultaneously with the election of Yuan Shih-kai as president.
ABOLITION OF FOREIGN SETTLEMENTS IN CHOSEN
The protocol abrogating the foreign settlements in Chosen, signed on April 20 the preceding year, is published.
Japan declares war on Germany and Austria.

The Chinese Government requested Japan January 8 to delimit the war zone in Shantung and withdraw her troops from that zone. Accordingly, Minister Hioki in Peking held a conference with Yuan Shih-kai on January 18 to discuss Japan's counter proposals. Japan served an ultimatum on May 6, and the Chinese Government accepted all the Japanese proposals.
Ratifications of a commercial treaty exchanged on July 10.
Japan participated on Oct. 19 in the agreement of the Allied powers signed in London prohibiting the signatories from concluding a separate peace with Germany.
Anticipating disturbances in connection with the apparent designs of Yuan Shih-kai to revive the Imperial government in China, Japan issued a warning to China on October 28.
The third Russo-Japanese agreement for protection of Japanese and Russian interests in the Far East signed on July 3.

Japan and the United States exchanged notes declaring that territorial propinquity created special relation between countries. This exchange of opinion, published on November 7, is generally known as the Ishii-Lansing Agreement.
Entente concluded on May 16, and its text published by the Japanese Foreign Office on May 30.
DECLARATION OF THE RENDITION OF SHANTUNG
Count Uchida, the Foreign Minister announced the restoration of complete Chinese sovereignty on May 17.
Prince Kimmochi Saionji signed the Versailles treaties at 3 o'clock in the afternoon of June 28.
DEMAND FOR THE EVACUATION OF SIBERIA
The Soviet Government of Irkutsk sent an ultimatum to Japan on March 11.
Japanese Government issued statement re withdrawal of troops.
Revision of regulations by the Immigration Bureau of the United States.
The Japanese and British Governments notified the Secretariat of the League of Nation on July 14, that the duration of the Anglo-Japanese alliance will be extended for another year.
REOPENING OF THE GERMAN EMBASSY IN TOKYO
Dr. Solf arrived in Japan as the first German ambassador after the Great War.
THE GENEVA TRI-PARTITE NAVAL DISARMAMENT CONFERENCE
Protocol signed whereby Japan extends de jure recognition to the new State.
Conference held at Simla and New Delhi, India.
New treaty signed at London, on July 12.
The New State was proclaimed "Empire" and Mr. Pu-yi endorsed as Emperor. March 1.
Conference adjourned on March 14 in failure.
Conference opened at Batavia on June 8 which adjourned on December 21 indefinitely.
Transference of North Manchuria Railway by the U.S.S.R. to Manchoukuo formally signed at Tokyo on March 23.
JAPAN'S WITHDRAWAL FROM THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS
THE VISIT OF THE EMPEROR OF MANCHOUKUO
The Emperor of Manchoukuo visited Japan and made a formal call upon the Emperor of Japan on April 6.
All demands of the Japanese garrison at Tientsin on various problems relating to North China accepted by the Nanking Government.
WITHDRAWAL FROM THE WASHINGTON NAVAL TREATY
Japanese Government notified the U.S.A. Government their intention to terminate the Washington Naval Treaty, December 29.
The Agreement guarding against the Communist International was entered into, between Japan and Germany on November 25, 1936.
Beginning of Sino-Japanese hostilities on July 7.
Beginning of the hostilities at Shanghai on August 13.
Occupation of Shanghai by Japanese forces on November 13.
Defeat of the Chinese armies at Suchow on May 19.
THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS ON THE CONFLICT
The League of Nations declared Japanese violation of the Nine Power Treaty on October 6, and Japan refuted it promptly.
A conference was convened at Brussels on the Sino-Japanese Conflict, and Japan was invited to the conference. But Japan rejected the invitation on October 27.
Italy entered the German-Japanese Agreement against the Comintern and the Tripartite Protocol made public on November 6.
Soviet forces occupied Changkufeng of Manchoukuo on July 12.
Hostilities between Japanese and Soviet forces ceased by the agreement concluded on August 10.
Canton was occupied by Japanese forces on October 21, and Wuhan cities on October 27.
Entrance of Manchoukuo and Hungary into the Agreement on February 24.
Spain's formal participation took place on March 27.
English and French Concessions blockaded by Japanese Army on June 14.
Tokyo Parley between Japan and Great Britain began on July 15.

title: Annual State Revenue and Expenditure
footnotes: Note:—(1) The financial year begins on April 1st and ends on March 31st.
(2) The figures for 1935-36 and the years preceding it represent the settled accounts.
(3) * Represent the actual account on July 31, 1937.
(4) ‡ Represent the budget.

(5) The gross surplus indicates the balance of revenue over expenditure for each financial year. Under the Budget and Account Act the surplus actually created in each financial year is transferred to the Budget of the succeeding year, and this Gross Surplus includes not only the accumulation brought forward from preceding financial years, but the net surplus actually created in that year. Accordingly, the balance of the gross and the net surplus represents a part or a total of the surplus created in the preceding year. Part of the gross surplus is applied to disbursements and deferred expenditures during the succeeding year and the balance is carried forward as a surplus to be used in succeeding financial years. The National Loan Redemption Act as amended in 1915 required redemption of the national debt up to 1.16% of the amount outstanding at the commencement of the preceding financial year. The same Act was further amended in 1927 to require an additional appropriation for the same purpose of not less than 25% of the surplus actually created in the year before the preceding one. The same Act as amended in 1932, however, provides that the amount to be applied to redemption of the national debt shall, for the time being, be over one-third of 1.16% of the total debts outstanding at the commencement of the preceding financial year, and that the additional appropriation for the same purpose of not less than 25% of the surplus actually created in the year before the preceding one may be suspended.
(6) As fractions not exceeding 1 yen are omitted, the totals of the figures and the grand total do not correspond. This explanation is applicable to the following tables.
